papers.what_it_is: A vendor educational web page (Quantum Computing Inc resource library lesson) explaining multibody interactions in optimization, with satisfiability, factoring and Hamming-code decoding examples.

assertions.value: The authors state that multibody interactions are very uncommon in physics, although relatively common in computing.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Multibody interactions versus many-body problems', page 1
quotes: they are very uncommon in physics, despite being relatively common in computing.

assertions.value: The authors state that the ability to implement multibody interactions directly is part of what makes their hardware powerful, and call direct implementation a unique aspect of their technology.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Multibody interactions versus many-body problems', page 1; Section 'Conclusion', page 1
quotes: The ability to directly implement such interactions is part of what makes our hardware powerful.
A unique aspect of our technology is that we can implement the multibody interactions directly.
assertions.reader_inference: A company describing its own product. The page gives no benchmark, timing or solution-quality data in support.

assertions.value: The authors state that the gravitational many-body problem involves only two-body interactions, because the force equation is a sum of forces between each pair of objects.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Multibody interactions versus many-body problems', page 1
quotes: The gravitational many-body problem, however, still only involves two-body interactions.
the equation for the forces can be written as a sum of forces between each pair of objects.

assertions.value: The authors state that Newton's third law is fundamentally a two-body statement, and that multibody interactions are hard to find in commonly encountered physics and therefore hard to engineer.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Multibody interactions versus many-body problems', page 1
quotes: Newton's third law of motion is fundamentally a two-body statement
the fact that they don't appear much in physics (even quantum physics) also makes multibody interactions hard to engineer.

assertions.value: The authors state that arbitrary logical statements can be built up from clauses that reference three bits, but not if each statement only mentions two.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Multibody interactions versus many-body problems', page 1
quotes: arbitrary logical statements can be built up from clauses that reference three bits, but not if each statement only mentions two.

assertions.value: The authors state that checking whether sums of many bits are even or odd is useful in error correction, and that the most natural statement of factoring a number into primes involves statements with terms over four bits.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Multibody interactions versus many-body problems', page 1
quotes: Checking whether sums of many bits are even or odd is useful in error correction
the most natural statement of the problem of factoring a number into primes involves statements with terms over four bits.

assertions.value: The authors give the avoidance of fire as an example of a fundamentally three-body logical statement: heat, air and fuel must not all be present together, but any two are fine.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Multibody interactions versus many-body problems', page 1
quotes: consider the three ingredients needed to start a fire: heat, air, and fuel.
but any two are fine.
a statement which fundamentally references three distinct conditions.

assertions.value: The authors define the order of interactions in an objective function as the maximum number of terms multiplied together, and call single terms linear and pairwise products quadratic.
quotes: what is the maximum number of terms multiplied together in the equations that express the problem?
Single terms are called linear and pairwise products are called quadratic.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines these terms in the first paragraph of the section.

assertions.value: The authors define a linear unconstrained binary optimization (LUBO) as defined similarly to a QUBO, with binary variables.
quotes: linear unconstrained binary optimization (LUBO, defined similarly to a QUBO
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition given in the text of the section.

assertions.value: The authors state that any purely linear objective function without constraints is easy to solve, since it is minimized by setting every variable with a negative prefactor to one and every variable with a positive prefactor to zero, and that such models are not commonly studied for that reason.
quotes: Without constraints, any purely linear objective function is easy to solve
the function could be minimized by just making all terms with a negative prefactor one and those with a positive prefactor zero.
LUBOs and any unconstrained linear models are not commonly studied because they are not very interesting.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument is informal; it is correct for binary variables with no constraints.

assertions.value: The authors state that linear problems with constraints can be computationally hard and of great interest, and that this is generally the field of linear programming.
quotes: Linear problems which include constraints can be computationally hard and of great interest; generally, this is the field of linear programming
assertions.reader_inference: Linear programming over continuous variables is solvable in polynomial time; the page's sentence is about constrained binary (integer) problems.

assertions.value: The authors state that QUBOs are known to be NP-hard, meaning that they can be mapped from any other optimization problem.
quotes: QUBOs are known to be NP-hard
assertions.reader_inference: The page glosses NP-hardness loosely (any NP problem reduces to a QUBO); the quoted gloss is the page's wording.

assertions.value: The authors give a three-variable quadratic example with two negative terms and one positive term, and state that the two negative terms cannot both reach their minimum without a penalty from the positive term; they call this competition frustration, and say it makes a general QUBO non-trivial to solve.
quotes: that is actually impossible without incurring a penalty from the positive term. This competition (known as frustration in the language of physics) makes it non-trivial to find the arrangement that solves a general QUBO.

assertions.value: The authors state that E = x1 x2 - x2 x3 - x1 x3 has minimum objective value -1 when x1 = x2 = x3 = 1.
quotes: E = x 1 x 2 − x 2 x 3 − x 1 x 3 E=x_1x_2-x_2x_3-x_1x_3 E = x 1 x 2 − x 2 x 3 − x 1 x 3 gives a minimum objective value of − 1 -1 − 1 when x 1 = x 2 = x 3 = 1

assertions.value: The authors state that NP-hardness means a QUBO can map anything, but that beyond a mild guarantee of not exploding exponentially, it does not guarantee how practical such mappings are.
quotes: By virtue of being NP-hard, we know that QUBOs can map anything, but beyond a relatively mild guarantee of not exploding exponentially, this doesn't guarantee how practical such mappings would be.

assertions.value: The authors state that strong second-order interactions can be used to implement constraints, and that higher-order terms come about naturally in many settings.
quotes: strong second-order interactions can be used to implement constraints.
It turns out higher-order terms of this form come about quite naturally in many settings.

assertions.value: The authors say a cited paper proposes mapping a product of three binary variables to lower order by adding a single additional variable, and a product of n variables by adding n such variables.
quotes: by adding a single additional variable
by adding n n n such variables.

assertions.value: The authors state that strong coupling is used to force the values of the additional (auxiliary) variables, so that their values are determined by the variables used for computation.
quotes: The idea is that strong coupling is used to force the values of the additional variables
so that their value is determined by the value of the variables that are actually used for computation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the third-order coupling mapping from a cited paper constrains the auxiliary variable to take the value of a majority vote, and that any third-order interaction can then be realized with linear penalties on the auxiliary together with the available quadratic and linear terms.
quotes: the third-order coupling mapping from this paper constrains the auxiliary variable to take the value of a majority vote.
any third-order interaction can be realized.

assertions.value: The authors state as a key takeaway that if only quadratic interactions are available, at least one auxiliary variable is needed per higher-order term, which can greatly grow the number of variables.
quotes: at least one auxiliary variable will be needed per higher-order term
This can greatly grow the number of variables needed to describe the problem
assertions.reader_inference: Stated as a takeaway without a proof or a count in the page.

assertions.value: The authors list two further disadvantages of mapping: the constraint couplings must be strong and on real devices could wash out the coupling that describes the objective function, and hardware solvers that update variables one at a time can be disrupted by an auxiliary variable that must pass through a high-energy intermediate configuration.
quotes: firstly, the couplings to implement the constraints must be strong.
if the couplings are made too strong they could wash out the coupling used to actually describe the objective function.
most hardware solvers work by updating variables one at a time, so adding an auxiliary variable that must also change its value can disrupt performance.

assertions.value: The authors state that on most platforms it is difficult to directly implement higher-than-quadratic interactions, and that many proposals for superconducting systems just use built-in auxiliary variables.
quotes: on most platforms, it is difficult to directly implement higher-than-quadratic interactions.
many proposals that have been made for implementing higher-order interactions in superconducting systems just use built-in auxiliary variables
assertions.reader_inference: The authors decline to explain the physical reasons ("too much of a digression into physics").

assertions.value: The authors say that one of the first instances of mapping high-order to low-order terms in the context of quantum annealing was to map a protein folding problem.
quotes: one of the first instances of mapping high-order to low-order terms in the context of quantum annealing was to map a protein folding problem

assertions.value: The authors state that satisfiability problems are conventionally written in conjunctive normal form (CNF).
quotes: Satisfiability problems are conventionally written in what is known as conjunctive normal form (CNF).
assertions.certainty_reason: Convention stated by the paper in the section's second paragraph.

assertions.value: The authors state that a satisfiability problem can be written as a polynomial in binary variables in which each clause is a product of terms that evaluates to one if the clause is violated and zero otherwise, and that any sum greater than zero indicates an unsatisfied clause.
quotes: each conjunctive clause can be written as a product of terms that evaluates to 1 if the clause is violated, and 0 otherwise.
any sum greater than 0 0 0 indicates that the clause is not satisfied.
assertions.reader_inference: The page calls clauses joined by OR "conjunctive" and the sum over clauses "disjunctive (AND)"; the usual terms are the reverse (clauses of ORs, joined by AND). The encoding itself is standard.

assertions.value: The authors state that the order of the interaction needed equals the number of variables combined by OR operations in a single clause.
quotes: the order of the interaction needed is equal to the number of variables, which are combined using O R OR OR operations in a single clause.

assertions.value: The authors state that two-satisfiability is not a hard computational problem, and that three-satisfiability was one of the first problems shown to be NP-complete and is often used in reductions to show NP-hardness, so third-order interactions give access to the interesting satisfiability problems.
quotes: Two-satisfiability, the version where each clause only involves two variables, is not a hard computational problem
Three-satisfiability, on the other hand, was one of the first problems shown to be NP-complete
third-order interactions allow us to access the interesting set of satisfiability problems.

assertions.value: The authors state that factoring is strongly suspected to not be NP-hard, that it is highly important in cryptography because most widely used cryptographic methods would be broken if it could be done efficiently for large numbers, and that Shor's algorithm was an early motivation for the field of quantum computing.
quotes: While strongly suspected to not be NP-hard, factoring is a highly important problem in cryptography
most widely used cryptographic methods would be broken if it could be done efficiently for large numbers.
was an early motivation for the field of quantum computing.

assertions.value: The authors state that factoring can be cast as minimizing the square of X1 X2 minus N, which reaches the minimum value of zero only when X1 and X2 are factors of N, and that the resulting expression is fourth order since it involves the product of squared terms.
quotes: Factoring can be cast as a minimization problem
This objective takes the minimum value of zero only when
The resulting expression, however, is fourth order since it involves the product of squared terms.

assertions.value: The authors state that their device has the capability of handling integer terms directly.
quotes: Note that our device has the capability of handling integer terms directly

assertions.value: The authors encode the factoring of 6 = 2 x 3 with each factor taking values up to three, written in a ones place and a twos place binary encoding, and state that the objective can be made equal to zero, encoding X1 = 2 and X2 = 3, the correct factorization.
quotes: we can encode the factoring of 6 = 2 × 3
each to take values of up to three, they can be written as
it is relatively straightforward to check that this expression can be made equal to zero by setting
this further encodes X 1 = 2 X_1=2 X 1 = 2 and X 2 = 3 X_2=3 X 2 = 3 , which is the correct factorization.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors check the zero by inspection and do not expand the expression. The setting printed for the second factor contains an index (x2(3)) that the two-bit encoding does not define, so it is a typographic slip in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that the binary factoring objective is a squared quadratic expression and so contains terms up to fourth order, and conclude that the most direct way of expressing factoring problems involves fourth-order terms.
quotes: It is also clear that it would involve terms up to fourth order since it is already a quadratic expression and is squared.
Therefore, the most direct way of expressing factoring problems involves fourth-order terms.

assertions.value: The authors state that parity check information is whether the sum of a set of bit values is odd or even, and that when bits are lost or flipped it is the most effective information to send.
quotes: When bits are lost or flipped, the most effective information to send is parity check information.
This information is whether the sum of a set of bit values is odd or even.

assertions.value: The authors state that with Ising variables z taking values one and minus one, defined from the binary variables x, the product of z variables equals minus one if the sum of the corresponding x variables is odd and one if it is even.
quotes: Unlike the previous examples, error correction decoding is most naturally expressed in terms of Ising variables
will be equal to − 1 -1 − 1 if x i + x j + . . . x_i+x_j+... x i + x j + ... is odd and 1 1 1 if it is even.

assertions.value: The authors state that, since the order of the interaction scales with the number of bits in the sum, decoding of error correction is fundamentally a multi-body problem.
quotes: since the order of the interaction scales with the number of bits in the sum, decoding of error correction is fundamentally a multi-body problem.

assertions.value: The authors consider decoding the Hamming [7,4] code, in which three parity checking bits, which may be subject to noise, can correct a single error on four transmitted bits, and in which a single corrupted parity check bit is correctly identified as needing no correction.
quotes: we consider decoding the famous Hamming [7,4] code, which is a code where three parity checking bits (also potentially subject to noise) can be used to correct a single error on four transmitted bits
(as well as correctly identifying that no correction is needed if a single parity check bit is corrupted)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the code and its correction property as the setup of its decoding example.

assertions.value: The authors define the three parity bits of the Hamming code as p1 = mod2(d1+d2+d4), p2 = mod2(d1+d3+d4) and p3 = mod2(d2+d3+d4), and the decoding task as determining the transmitted bits that correspond to the least number of bit flip errors.
quotes: p_1=\mathrm{mod}_2(d_1+d_2+d_4)
p_2=\mathrm{mod}_2(d_1+d_3+d_4)
p_3=\mathrm{mod}_2(d_2+d_3+d_4)
The task of decoding is then to determine the original transmitted bits that correspond to the least number of bit flip errors occurring.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definitions printed in the paper's Hamming [7,4] example.

assertions.value: The authors give an energy function over Ising variables, with linear terms in the four data bits and cubic terms z1 z2 z4, z1 z3 z4 and z2 z3 z4 weighted by the parity bits, to be minimized after all seven bits are received.
quotes: Having received all seven bits, the task of decoding consists of minimizing
assertions.reader_inference: The page does not run the minimization; it argues by inspection.

assertions.value: The authors argue by inspection of the energy function that each z value appears in at least two of the three parity strings, so a single flipped bit makes assigning a value other than the original energetically more costly, and a single corrupted parity check is overridden by the other parity checks and the transmitted bit value, so the code does not erroneously correct a value.
quotes: By inspecting this formula we can see how the error correction works.
it would end up being energetically more costly to assign a value other than the original one, thus, allowing the original bitstring to be recovered.
the code would not erroneously "correct" a value if a single parity check were corrupted.
assertions.reader_inference: An inspection argument without a proof or a run. For data bit one, the linear term and two cubic terms hold it; the argument for the all-values statement is not worked out in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that error correction can achieve close to the best theoretically allowed behavior in practice because of turbo codes, whose decoding corresponds to an easy optimization rather than a hard one, and that low-density parity-check codes, proposed decades earlier, were later realized to have the same property.
quotes: Error correction is commonly used in communication in practice, and can achieve close to the best theoretically allowed behavior.
turbo codes , where the decoding problem corresponds to an easy optimization, rather than a hard one.
low-density parity-check codes , which were proposed decades earlier had the same property

assertions.value: The authors state that there may still be niche applications, such as quantum error correction, where a different code must be used and the correction does correspond to a hard optimization problem.
quotes: there may still be niche applications where one might have to use a different code for some reason
one where the correction does correspond to a hard optimization problem.
assertions.reader_inference: By the authors' own account, the widely used codes (turbo, low-density parity-check) give easy decoding, so the Hamming example illustrates a multi-body problem form rather than a case where multibody hardware has an advantage.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that multibody interactions can be mapped to two-body interactions, but this process involves at least an extra variable per interaction and may reduce solving efficiency, and that their technology implements multibody interactions directly.
quotes: While multibody interactions can be mapped to two-body interactions, this process will involve at least an extra variable per interaction, and may reduce solving efficiency.
A unique aspect of our technology is that we can implement the multibody interactions directly.
assertions.reader_inference: No measured comparison between native multibody and mapped two-body solving is given on the page.

papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc educational web page relating neural networks to the reservoir computing paradigm and arguing that reservoir computing reduces training cost.

assertions.value: The page states that artificial neural networks are an artificial intelligence paradigm loosely inspired by how biological neural networks work, and calls the comparison a vast oversimplification that is conceptually accurate at a very abstract level.
quotes: Artificial neural networks are an artificial intelligence paradigm that is loosely inspired by how biological neural networks work naturally.
This is, of course, a vast oversimplification of how brains and learning work but conceptually accurate at a very abstract level.
assertions.certainty_reason: An educational statement without evidence in the page.

assertions.value: The company states that most implementations of reservoir computers, including its own, can be viewed as types of artificial neural networks, and that recurrent neural networks are the class many reservoir systems formally belong to.

quotes: Most implementations of reservoir computers, including ours, can be viewed as types of artificial neural networks.
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), the class of neural networks that many reservoir systems formally belong to
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing its own product class.

assertions.value: The page states that tensors used in machine learning are a special case of mathematics and physics tensors, behave like matrices or vectors given extra dimensions for bookkeeping, and have linear mathematics, whereas mathematics and physics tensors of dimension three or higher can represent non-linear interactions.
assertions.anchor: Linear operations and tensors section, web page
quotes: In mathematics and physics a tensor with dimension three or higher can be used to represent non-linear interactions
machine learning tensors are more like matrices or vectors which have been given more dimensions for bookkeeping purposes, but their mathematics is linear.

assertions.value: The page defines the basic linear operations in neural networks as adding and subtracting numbers, possibly weighted, and says any set of linear equations can be represented as a matrix.
assertions.anchor: Linear operations and tensors section, web page
quotes: The basic operations to move this information around are known as linear operations, adding and subtracting numbers, possibly in a weighted way
Any set of linear equations can be represented as a matrix, a two-dimensional array of numbers
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states its own definition of linear operations in the Linear operations and tensors section.

assertions.value: The page states that a purely linear neural network, of any size, can be collapsed into a set of linear equations giving the outputs in terms of the inputs, so it needs some nonlinearity to reliably perform sophisticated tasks.
quotes: if we build a purely linear neural network, no matter how big it is, it can always just be collapsed into a set of linear equations describing the outputs in terms of the inputs.
For an artificial neural network to be able to reliably perform sophisticated tasks like recognizing cats, it needs some nonlinearity.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated informally without a proof in the page.

assertions.value: The page describes a rectified linear unit (ReLU) as a node that sets its input to zero if it is negative and leaves it unchanged if it is positive, and says almost any form of nonlinearity can in principle supply the needed complexity.

In this way, it is effectively removed from the network.

papers.what_it_is: A vendor educational web lesson from Quantum Computing Inc explaining linear versus nonlinear mathematical models and why nonlinear optics is needed for quantum optics and reservoir systems.

assertions.value: The lesson states that a mathematical model is linear when its solutions obey the property of superposition, and nonlinear when they do not.
quotes: The question of whether a mathematical model is linear essentially asks whether the solutions obey the property of superposition. Linear models obey this property and nonlinear models do not.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines linearity this way in its second section.

assertions.value: The authors state that a completely linear neural network, no matter how large, could be described by simple matrix-vector multiplication, and that even simple nonlinearity makes a neural network much more powerful.
quotes: a completely linear neural network, no matter how large, could be described by simple matrix-vector multiplication
even simple nonlinearity can make a neural network much more powerful
assertions.reader_inference: A standard textbook point; the lesson gives no proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that neural networks need some nonlinearity to be suitable for sophisticated learning tasks.
quotes: neural networks need some nonlinearity to be suitable for sophisticated learning tasks

assertions.value: The authors state that differentiation is a linear operation, so the derivative of a sum of two functions equals the sum of their derivatives, and that arbitrarily high-order derivatives also obey superposition.
quotes: so differentiation is a linear operation
Since higher-order derivatives are defined by repeatedly applying the same definition, arbitrarily high-order derivatives also obey superposition.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states the property as part of its account of a linear differential equation.

assertions.value: The authors state that a differential equation involving only sums of constants, first powers of a variable, and arbitrarily high derivatives of that variable is linear, and that terms such as the square of the variable, the product of the variable with its derivative, and the square of the derivative are nonlinear.
quotes: any differential equation involving sums of constants, first powers of a variable
will be linear.
are nonlinear.
assertions.reader_inference: The three nonlinear terms are printed as LaTeX in the text layer, so the quotes hold only the connecting words.

assertions.value: The authors state that the presence of any nonlinear terms makes the entire differential equation nonlinear.
quotes: The presence of any nonlinear terms makes the entire differential equation nonlinear.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a rule of the definition.

assertions.value: The authors state that nonlinearity is a mathematical property, not a physical one, and that calling a physical system linear or nonlinear is a convenient shorthand that is not mathematically rigorous.
quotes: It is important to remember that nonlinearity is a mathematical property, not a physical one.
Such terminology, however, is not mathematically rigorous, it is just a convenient shorthand.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson states how it uses the terms.

assertions.value: The authors state that linear systems of differential equations tend to be much easier to solve than nonlinear systems, because new solutions can be built by summing known solutions.
quotes: Mathematically, linear systems of differential equations tend to be much easier to solve than nonlinear systems.
new solutions can be built by summing up already known solutions

assertions.value: The authors give matrix diagonalization as an example: a complete set of eigenvectors is generated and summed to solve how a system behaves from any starting point, and they state that such techniques do not work for nonlinear systems of equations.
quotes: a technique known as matrix diagonalization where a complete set of eigenvectors
Such techniques do not work for nonlinear systems of equations.

assertions.value: The authors present the Lorenz attractor as a solution to the nonlinear Lorenz equations of fluid dynamics, where superposition does not work and two very similar starting conditions diverge quickly in time.
quotes: a Lorenz attractor , which arises as a solution to a set of nonlinear differential equations known as the Lorenz equations which arise in fluid dynamics
In fact, the difference between two very similar starting conditions will grow quickly in time until their behavior is very different.

assertions.value: The authors state that linear equations can never have chaotic solutions, although nonlinear equations will not always have chaotic solutions.

assertions.value: The authors state that the same system can sometimes be described in both a linear and a nonlinear way, which is not a paradox because physical models are approximations, and that the linearity of the model depends on which approximations are made.

The linearity or nonlinearity of the model depends on which approximations are made.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as the lesson's framing of what the terms apply to.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Schroedinger equation is linear in quantum amplitudes, the summing of which describes quantum interference, but that the number of states in multi-particle systems tends to grow exponentially with the number of particles, so the linear equation quickly becomes too large to solve.

the number of possible states described in multi-particle quantum systems tends to grow exponentially with the number of particles

assertions.value: The authors state that nonlinear optics can be described in a quantum mechanical, technically linear way, but that the practical description is often in terms of light particles rather than amplitudes, and that in nonlinear optics the light particles do not obey superposition.
quotes: While nonlinear optics can be described in a quantum mechanical (and technically linear) way
In nonlinear optics, the light particles do not obey superposition and are therefore not described in a linear way.

assertions.value: The authors state that nonlinear optics studies how light interacts with materials to produce effects that depend on the light's intensity, making these effects nonlinear in relation to the strength of the underlying fields.

increasing the light intensity will only lead to brighter light

nonlinear equations cannot be solved in this way

papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc educational web lesson giving a high-level overview of quantum optics, non-linear optics, interference, the Hong-Ou-Mandel effect and the company's lithium niobate chip approach.

assertions.value: The page states that weakening the strength of a light source such as a laser or a light bulb does not make quantum effects apparent, even when a pulse holds on average a single photon or less.
quotes: just weakening the strength of a light source such as a laser or a light bulb does not make quantum effects apparent.
This is even the case if it is weakened so much that on average a pulse of light only contains a single particle (photon), or even less than one.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement in a vendor's educational page; the page gives no proof and defers the mathematical explanation.
assertions.reader_inference: This is standard physics (a weak coherent state stays classical-like), stated here without derivation.

assertions.value: The page defines non-linear optics, in its use, as the case where photons are allowed to interact with each other through an underlying material, which lets the company turn ordinary light such as laser light into more interesting types of light.
quotes: Non-linear optics addresses cases where photons are allowed to interact with each other through an underlying material.
This allows us to turn more mundane types of light, such as those produced by a laser, into more interesting types of light.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page's own definition of the term it relies on, Non-linear optics section.

assertions.value: The page states that without interactions between photons the company can produce pulses with one particle on average but cannot produce a pulse known for sure to have exactly one, and that interaction through a non-linear medium overcomes this limit.
quotes: Without interactions between them, the particles will act independently, with no influence from the other ones
we can produce pulses where there is one particle on average , but not produce a pulse that we know for sure has exactly one.
If light particles are able to interact through a non-linear medium it is clear to see that this limitation can be overcome.
assertions.certainty_reason: A conceptual argument in a vendor's educational page, without derivation.
assertions.reader_inference: The page's claim that interaction in a medium is needed for a known exact photon number is a simplification; heralded single-photon sources are the usual route and also rely on non-linear processes.

quotes: Quantum superposition allows a system to effectively explore many possibilities in parallel, although it is only useful if we can also couple it with quantum interference.

papers.version_note: The text is a saved web page of a vendor lesson (site navigation first, then the lesson, then a link list). The text layer has no page breaks, so it is treated as one page. Some inline citations lost their subject in the text layer (for example the sentence on power consumption starts with the bare reference number 7).
papers.what_it_is: A vendor primer from Quantum Computing Inc that explains what a qudit is, how superposition and interference are used, and how qudits are used in its feedback-based entropy quantum computing (EQC) analog optimizer.

assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own paradigm; the lesson gives no technical detail of it.

assertions.value: The authors state that their qudit-based paradigm allows them to work in a traditional binary setting or to explore integer models, and to some extent continuous models.
assertions.anchor: Doing What Qubits Can Do Plus More, last sentence
quotes: Our qudit-based paradigm allows the flexibility to both work in a traditional binary setting or to explore what can be done with integer (and too some extent continuous) models
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes the flexibility of its own paradigm.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike bits in a conventional computer, qubits and qudits take on multiple values at the same time, which they call superposition, and that during computation each qudit takes on multiple values at the same time, enabling greater exploration of a problem search space.
quotes: Unlike information encoded using bits in a conventional computer, qubits and qudits take on multiple values at the same time. This is called superpostion.
each qudit will take on multiple values at the same time, enabling greater exploration of a problem search space
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines superposition in its own words in the Superposition section.
assertions.reader_inference: The phrase 'multiple values at the same time' is a popular simplification; a superposition is a weighted sum of basis states with amplitudes.

assertions.value: The authors describe a quantum die as an example of a qudit: for a six-sided die, the superposition of states is a sum of amplitudes alpha one to alpha six, each multiplying the ket of one face.
quotes: think of a quantum die. Six sides, for common dice the superposition of states would be described by:
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson writes the state of its quantum die example in the Superposition section.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson does not state the normalization condition on the amplitudes.

assertions.value: The authors give a worked example: the quadratic function f(x) minus two x one squared minus two x two squared plus x one times x two, over a domain from 0 to 99 for each variable, has two solutions at the same minimum value under the constraint that x one plus x two equals 99. The solutions [99, 0] and [0,99] give f equal to minus 19602.
quotes: has two solutions at the same minimum value under the constraint x 1 + x 2 = 99
These solutions ` [99, 0] ` and ` [0,99] ` result in f ( x ) = − 19602
assertions.certainty_reason: A worked arithmetic example given by the authors in a vendor primer; it is not run on hardware.
assertions.reader_inference: Checked by hand: on the constraint the function equals minus 19602 plus five times x one times x two, so the minimum is at the two end points, as stated. The lesson does not say which of two readings of the sentence 'minimum value' it uses (over the constraint line), but this reading is the one that fits.

assertions.value: The authors state that the example states are potentially evaluated at the same time in superposition, so that when a state is read multiple times from the system, both solutions should appear with the same frequency, and that other states such as [1, 98], [98, 1], [49, 50] and [50, 49] also exist in the superposition.
quotes: are potentially evaluated at the same time, so when a state is read multiple times from the system, both solutions should appear with the same frequency
Not only do these states exist in superposition, but also ` [1, 98] `, ` [98, 1] `, ` [49, 50] `, ` [50, 49] `, and so on.
assertions.certainty_reason: An illustrative statement by the authors; no device run is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: This describes an unbiased superposition; the lesson does not say that the device prepares it.

assertions.value: The authors state that superposition by itself is not useful for optimization: if measured, any of the answers would be equally likely, so the device would effectively be a random number generator, which they call another of their products.
quotes: By itself this superposition isn't actually useful for optimization, if we measured it we would be equally likely to measure any of the answers it would effectively be a random number generator (another one of our products).
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that to use a device as a quantum optimizer, the potential solutions must be interfered so that less optimal solutions cancel out and more optimal solutions reinforce, and that using interference is at the heart of all quantum optimisation techniques.
quotes: we need to interfere these potential solutions in such a way that less optimal solutions cancel out, and more optimal solutions reinforce
Using interference in a clever way to get good solutions is at the heart of all quantum optimisation techniques
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement by the authors without proof or citation in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that optical techniques have the advantage that they can also take advantage of non-linear optical effects, for example to amplify signals.
quotes: optical techniques have the advantage that they can also take advantage of non-linear optical effects, for example, to amplify signals
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes the advantage of its own technology class; no data is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that, depending on the device, sub-optimal solutions may appear with various frequency; that a solution state is read with a certain probability; and that crafting an objective function is about increasing the likelihood that a desirable state is read.
quotes: Depending on the device, sub-optimal solutions may appear with various frequency.
A solution state is read from the device with a certain probability and crafting an objective function is about increasing the likelyhood that a desireable state is read.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state in the Superposition section that the readout of the device is probabilistic and can return sub-optimal solutions.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson does not report how often sub-optimal solutions appear on any device.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum superposition is different from and more powerful than standard classical probability distributions, because classical probabilities can only add while quantum amplitudes can add or subtract, and that this ability to subtract is the interference phenomenon.
quotes: Quantum superposition, explained conceptually in [ 6 ], is different from and more powerful than standard classical probability distributions
while classical probabilities can only add, quantum amplitudes can add or subtract. This ability to subtract is the interference phenomena
assertions.certainty_reason: A conceptual explanation that the authors cite to another source; no proof in the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement is a standard textbook point; 'more powerful' is not defined in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum superpositions are fragile and can be destroyed by measurement, which converts them into ordinary probability distributions, so quantum devices and algorithms need to be designed to preserve the superpositions until the result is read out.
quotes: Quantum superpositions are fragile, and can be destroyed by measurement, which converts them into ordinary probability distributions.
quantum devices and algorithms need to be designed carefully in a way which preserves these superpositions until the result is read out
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of quantum superposition in the Superposition section.

assertions.value: The authors state that feedback-based EQC is an analog system. In an analog computer, a physical model represents a mathematical one through the initialization of physical states, the physical system evolves until a stopping condition is reached, and the measurements are then translated into values in the domain of the mathematical model.
quotes: Feedback-based EQC is an analog system, which defines how a qudit is leveraged to perform computation.
This physical system evolves until a stopping condition is reached, then the measurements of the system are translated into values in the domain of the mathematical model.
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines its analog computing model in the Analog System section.

assertions.value: The authors state that one of the most attractive benefits of analog computing at nanoscale is low power consumption. They state that cited devices consume power during operation on the order of a Mac Pro at idle, about 50W. The text layer lost the name of the devices, so the subject of the sentence is missing.
quotes: One of the most attractive benefits of analog computing at nanoscale is the miserly power consumption.
consume power during operation on the order of the consumption of a Mac Pro at idle (~50W)[ 8 ].
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor power figure that rests on two citations (reference 7 for the devices, reference 8 for the Mac Pro figure) and is not measured in the lesson; the subject is lost in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence has no stated device, so the figure cannot be tied to the Dirac-1 or any other product from this text alone. The link list names the Dirac-1 Technical Brief, which may be reference 7.

assertions.value: The authors state that a critical aspect of computing with qudits on analog devices is the translation of the measurements to the domain of the problem, which they call decoding. Measurements may be discrete, such as counting photon arrivals, or continuous, such as recording volumes of fluid.
quotes: is the translation of the measurements to the domain of the problem. This can be referred to as "decoding".
discrete measurements could be counting events such as photon arrivals and continuous measurements could be recording volumes of fluid
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines decoding in the Computation section.

assertions.value: The authors state that counts of photons in certain modes are translated to a mathematical model by relative intensity or a binary response; that unless the mathematical model has a 1-to-1 mapping with the photon counts, the meaning in the solution will likely be in a continuous domain; and that approximation methods can be used to convert between continuous and discrete or vice versa.
quotes: counts of photons in certain modes are translated to a mathematical model by relative intensity or a binary response
unless the mathematical model has a 1-to-1 mapping with the photon counts, the meaning in the solution will likely be in a continuous domain
approximation methods can be used to convert between continuous and discrete or vice versa
assertions.certainty_reason: A description by the authors without a worked decoding or data.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson does not say which decoding Dirac-1 uses.

assertions.value: The authors state that n qudits with dimensionality k translate to a solution vector of size n, with each element having k possible values, and that the number of variables is the most common measure of the size of a model.
quotes: The most common measure of the size of a model is the number of variables
n n n qudits with dimensionality k k k will translate to a solution vector of size n n n , with each element having k k k possible values
assertions.certainty_reason: The lesson defines the relation between qudit count, dimensionality and solution vector in the Qudit Dimensionality section.

assertions.value: The authors state that when taking l samples to test the effect of superposition, fewer than l distinct vectors will be produced, and each vector will appear fewer than l times. The lesson gives no measured sample.
quotes: When taking l l l samples to test the effect of superposition, m < l m<l m < l distinct vectors will be produced
assertions.certainty_reason: A generic statement by the authors without an experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: As written, the statement that fewer than l distinct vectors always appear is not guaranteed for any finite l; it holds only when some vector repeats. The lesson gives no condition.

assertions.value: The authors state in the conclusion that the primer has described what qudits are in relation to EQC, the power made possible through superposition, their use in analog computation, and the translation between a physical system and a mathematical model.
quotes: This primer on qudits has described what qudits are in relation to EQC, the power made possible through superposition, their use in analog computation and translation between a physical system and a mathematical model.
assertions.certainty_reason: The conclusion states the scope of the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson contains no experimental result, benchmark or hardware figure of merit.
